one_liner: State-machine compiler that generates FSM-based scanners/parsers in 13 host languages; beats flex on one old, unmeasured example.
what_it_does: Ragel compiles regular-expression and state-chart specifications into executable finite state machines emitted as source code in C, C++, D, Java, Ruby, C#, Go, OCaml, Rust, Julia, Zig, JavaScript, or GNU ASM x86-64. Unlike flex, action code is written inline in the host language and embedded directly into the generated state machine rather than kept in separate lex-style rule/action blocks. It is not a drop-in for a flex .l file: you write grammars in Ragel's own %%{ machine ... }%% syntax and choose a codegen backend (table-driven, flat table, or goto-driven) per use case.
how_it_is_fast: The goto-driven backends (-G0/-G1/-G2) generate direct branches between states with action code inlined at each transition, instead of flex's table-driven lookup-and-dispatch loop, trading generated code size for fewer indirections per input byte. Ragel also offers table-driven (-T0/-T1) and flat-table (-F0/-F1) backends for a size/speed tradeoff. The only concrete comparison found is a 2004-era changelog note (Ragel 3.7) that its C++ tokenizer example ran faster than an equivalent flex version but slower than a re2c version, with no numbers given.
when_to_use: You need one grammar to generate scanners/parsers for multiple host languages (e.g. C, Go, Rust, Zig) without maintaining separate lexers per language
You're building a hand-tunable, embeddable tokenizer where you want inlined action code and control over table vs. goto-driven codegen (as HarfBuzz and Puma's http11 parser do)
You want a long-lived, still-maintained lexer generator over one that's effectively archived (original ragel repo is archived; development continues here)
You're comfortable learning a dedicated grammar/action-code DSL instead of reusing an existing flex .l file
when_not_to_use: You need a numbers-backed performance case against flex: the only comparison here is a 22-year-old, non-numeric changelog claim (Tier D evidence)
You have an existing flex grammar and want a mechanical drop-in swap; Ragel's syntax and action-embedding model are different enough to require a rewrite
You need re2c-class speed specifically: Ragel's own changelog says it did not beat re2c on the one example checked
You need CI-verified support beyond x86-64 Linux; the project's GitHub Actions matrix only builds on ubuntu-latest, so other platforms/architectures are unverified here
You want to avoid a bootstrap toolchain: building Ragel from source requires building Colm first, since Ragel's frontend is written in Colm

integration.dependencies: none for generated code beyond the chosen host language's standard runtime; building the ragel compiler itself needs make, libtool, gcc, g++, autoconf, automake (or CMake 3.16+)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (no minimum C/C++ standard stated for generated code; build-from-source requires autotools or CMake 3.16+)
integration.platforms: CI covers x86-64 Linux only (GitHub Actions, ubuntu-latest); changelog references macOS build fixes (7.1.0, Aug 2026); no aarch64 CI observed

gotchas: Ragel's frontend is written in Colm, so building from source bootstraps Colm first, not just Ragel
Generated code style is chosen per grammar via compiler flag (table/flat-table/goto-driven, -T/-F/-G), so speed vs. code-size is a build-time decision, not automatic
The original standalone adrian-thurston/ragel GitHub repo is archived; active development moved to this adrian-thurston/colm-suite monorepo
The flex/re2c comparison lives in examples/, not in the project's test suite, and has never been rerun or updated with numbers since 2004
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Ragel over the numbers-backed siblings (LRSTAR's ~2x, simd-lexing's ~6.8x, CrossDB's ~10x, all vs. flex) when you need multi-target-language codegen and a widely-deployed, actively maintained generator rather than a project with an actual measured speedup; for a documented numeric win over flex specifically, LRSTAR or simd-lexing have real benchmark data and Ragel does not.
verified_claims_summary: The only comparison is an author's changelog entry for Ragel 3.7 (Oct 31, 2004): a C++ tokenizer example (examples/cppscan) was implemented three ways -- Ragel, flex, and re2c -- and the Ragel version was reported to run faster than the flex version but slower than the re2c version, with no numbers, no stated compiler flags, and no hardware given.
status_note: Actively maintained under the colm-suite umbrella with a commit on 2026-09-25 and a 7.1.0 release (Aug 2026) adding Zig support; MIT licensed and small enough to vendor, but the original standalone ragel repo is archived so colm-suite is the current canonical home.
